runs.u: Can you recommend a messaging app?
runs.reply:
There's no universal best one — the right choice depends almost entirely on what you prioritise, and who you need to talk to. I'll break down the common options by actual real-world use case:

---
### 1. 🔒 If privacy is your #1 priority: **Signal**
- This is the current gold standard for private messaging. Default end-to-end encryption for *everything* (1:1 chats, groups, calls, even statuses), fully open source, collects effectively zero user data, no ads, no tracking.
- Downsides: Almost no extra fun or utility features, and critically: it only works if everyone you are chatting with also agrees to install it. Most people will not switch just for you.
- Good for: Sensitive conversations, talking with other privacy-conscious people.

---
### 2. ⚡ If you want features, speed and utility: **Telegram**
- Blazing fast, works simultaneously on every device (phone, laptop, tablet even if your main phone is turned off), permanent cloud chat history, 2GB free file uploads, 200,000 person groups, custom bots, public communities and endless customisation.
- Downsides: Normal cloud chats are **not end-to-end encrypted by default**. You have to manually start a separate 'secret chat' for encrypted conversations, and those will not sync across devices.
- Good for: Large group chats, sharing files, hobby communities, casual work coordination.

---
### 3. 🤷 If you just need to talk to normal people: **WhatsApp**
- 9 out of 10 people you will ever need to message already have this installed. Default end-to-end encryption for chats, extremely reliable, dead simple interface.
- Downsides: Owned by Meta, collects and shares huge amounts of metadata, business spam is getting out of hand, and ad targeting is creeping further into the product every year.
- This is the default you will end up using regardless. There is no practical way around it for most everyday social contact.

---
### 4. 🛠️ For teams / dedicated groups:
- **Slack** for formal professional teams, best in class for work tool integrations
- **Discord** for hobby groups, gaming, and casual teams, has far better persistent voice/video than every other app on this list.

---
One final very real note: The most secure messaging app in the world is completely useless if the person you want to talk to will not install it. Almost everyone ends up running 2-3 of these side by side for different groups of people.

runs.u: Can you recommend a messaging app?
runs.reply:
I'll split these by what you actually need most -- there's no universal best messenger, just the best one for your priorities:

---
### 🔒 If privacy & security is your #1 concern
1.  **Signal**
    The default sensible choice: fully open source, zero-knowledge architecture, *default end-to-end encryption* for every single one-on-one chat, group chat and call. Collects effectively zero user metadata. Only real downside is it has much lower adoption than WhatsApp/Telegram.

    Currently the most mathematically private messenger that exists. It does not assign any user ID at all, not even an anonymous one. For people who want actual unlinkable communication. It is slightly clunky for daily casual use.

    No phone number required to sign up, runs on a distributed network instead of central servers. Good if you do not want to tie your chat identity to your phone at all.

---
### 🧑🤝🧑 For regular daily use / most of your contacts already use it
1.  **Telegram**
    Blazing fast, infinite cloud chat history, best-in-class file sharing (send up to 2GB free without compression), extremely powerful bots, almost unlimited customisation. *Very important note:* normal chats are **not end-to-end encrypted by default** -- you have to manually start a Secret Chat, and group chats never get E2EE at all.
2.  **WhatsApp**
    Almost universal adoption, default E2EE now, zero learning curve. Big downside: it is owned by Meta, and logs extensive metadata about who you talk to, when, and how often for ad targeting.

---
### 💼 For groups, hobby communities or work teams
1.  **Discord**
    Unbeatable voice chat, screenshare, role permissions and thread organisation for groups. Perfect for friend circles, game clans or hobby communities.
2.  **Element**
    Open source, built on the Matrix protocol, properly E2EE for teams, can be self hosted, and can even bridge into all your other chat apps in one place.

---

What are you prioritising most right now? Privacy? That all your existing contacts will have it? File sharing? Team features?

runs.u: Can you recommend a ride-hailing app?
runs.reply:
The best ride-hailing app depends heavily on your location, local regulations, and what you prioritize (price, safety, wait times, vehicle options). Here are reliable common options sorted by region, along with practical notes:
---
### Major Trusted Options By Region
1.  **Uber**
    Available in ~70 countries, the most widely supported option for international travel. Features consistent upfront pricing, built-in live trip sharing, and an in-app emergency button. Note that surge pricing during peak hours can increase fares drastically.
2.  **Lyft**
    Primary alternative for the USA & Canada. Generally has more transparent pricing policies than Uber in most North American markets, and typically has better reviewed driver working conditions.
3.  **Didi Chuxing**
    Dominant service in mainland China, also operates in parts of Latin America, Russia and Africa. Has an extremely large driver pool resulting in very short wait times in most urban areas.
4.  **Grab**
    The standard platform for Southeast Asia (Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam etc). Uniquely integrates ride hailing, food delivery, local e-wallet services and transport booking all in one application.
5.  **Bolt**
    Very popular across Europe, Africa and Central Asia. Almost always significantly cheaper than Uber for equivalent rides, with good urban coverage in most operating cities.
---
### Critical Advice Before Choosing Any App
-   First verify the app holds official local operating licenses for your city. Unregulated unlicensed platforms carry major safety risks.
-   If multiple apps work in your area, compare upfront price quotes for the same journey before booking -- fares can differ 20-40% between platforms at the exact same time.
-   For safety: always enable trip sharing with a contact, confirm the driver name and vehicle license plate before entering, and never get into an unmarked car.

There is no single "best" app that works well everywhere; always check recent local user reviews for your specific city first.

runs.u: Can you recommend a news outlet?
runs.reply:
First, critical preface: **There is no 100% unbiased news outlet**. Every organisation has editorial priorities, institutional biases, audience incentives and blind spots. The single best practice is never rely on only one source, and always cross-verify major claims across outlets with differing editorial positions.

Below are recommendations sorted by use case, with clear notes on their strengths and limitations:
---
### 🔹 For baseline fact-first breaking news
These are the primary sources that almost all other news outlets ultimately cite for events:
- *Associated Press (AP) / Reuters*: The global independent wire services. They prioritise confirming facts before publishing, run almost no editorial framing on main news feeds, and issue public, dated corrections. Weakness: they can be overly neutral to a fault, sometimes just restating conflicting claims without adding necessary context of harm or track record.
- *BBC News*: Generally reliable for international events outside UK domestic politics, with better on-the-ground context than raw wires. Has documented biases around UK government policy and coverage of regions with British colonial history.

---
### 🔹 For accountability & investigative work
- *ProPublica* (US focus): Non-profit, no advertising revenue. Almost every major US institutional accountability story of the last 15 years was either led by them or built on their work. They publish full methodology and raw source data where possible.
- *Bellingcat* (global): Pioneered open source digital investigation. They are fully transparent about exactly how they reached every conclusion, rather than citing anonymous sources. They hold explicit editorial stances against authoritarianism and war crimes.

---
### 🔹 For editorial perspectives (read these *alongside* each other)
It is healthy to regularly consume reporting from outlets you know do not align with your default views:
- Center-right mainstream: *The Wall Street Journal* **news section only** - note their opinion page is an extremely partisan separate operation
- Center-left mainstream: *The Washington Post*, *The Guardian*
- Left analysis: *Jacobin*
- Conservative non-populist analysis: *The Dispatch*

---
### Final ground rules:
1.  Always separate an outlet's news reporting team from their opinion/commentary team - these are almost always completely separate departments with no editorial oversight over one another
2.  Avoid algorithmic feeds that only show you content you will agree with
3.  If a claim is only being reported by one single outlet, it is not confirmed yet

runs.u: Can you recommend a news outlet?
runs.reply:
First, critical baseline reality: there is no 100% unbiased news outlet. All have editorial lean, institutional incentives, and blind spots. The only good habit is to never rely on only one source.

That said, here are reputable options sorted by what you actually need, with their known flaws and biases stated clearly:
---
### 1. For baseline factual "what actually happened" reporting (minimum editorializing)
These are the original wire services that almost every other outlet cites for core facts:
- **AP News**: Extremely conservative about running unconfirmed information, almost no inserted opinion in main news coverage. Lean: slightly center-right on economic matters, broadly centrist on social issues. Weak spot: can be overly deferential to official government sources.
- **Reuters**: Similar standard, stronger international coverage. Lean: dead center establishment. Weak spot: will sometimes invent false balance between mainstream and fringe claims for the sake of appearing neutral.
---
### 2. For good international on-the-ground coverage
- **BBC News**: Has the largest global correspondent network of any English language outlet. Lean: western establishment centrist, inherent pro-UK state bias. Weak spot: notoriously unreliable on UK domestic government scandals, unaddressed post-colonial blind spots in coverage of the global south.
---
### 3. For accountability investigative journalism
- **ProPublica**: Non-profit, no advertiser or corporate owner pressure. Runs the most consistent, well-documented accountability reporting in the US. Lean: clearly center-left, but they will aggressively investigate Democratic politicians when the facts are there.
- **Bellingcat**: Open-source independent investigators, unmatched at verifying war zone events, disinformation and state coverups. Lean: explicitly pro-transparency, anti-authoritarian, they publish their full editorial value statement publicly.
---
### What to never use as your primary source
Any outlet built around primetime opinion hosts (Fox prime, MSNBC prime, all partisan YouTube news channels, viral social media accounts). These products are not designed to inform you - they are designed to make you angry and keep you consuming.

Most importantly: for any major story, read at minimum two outlets with different editorial leanings. Do not pick one "home team" outlet that you trust for everything.

runs.u: Can you recommend a news outlet?
runs.reply:
There is no 100% unbiased news source. Every outlet makes conscious editorial choices about which stories to cover, how to frame events, and which voices get platformed. The healthiest approach is almost always to cross-read multiple outlets rather than picking one single "trusted" source.

Below are commonly cited options, documented with their known tendencies, strengths and tradeoffs, sorted by use case:

---
### 1. For basic factual updates, low editorializing
These are the newswires that almost all other outlets source their raw information from:
- **Associated Press (AP)**: Global, extremely fast on breaking events, almost never adds partisan framing to their straight news reports.
  ✅ Standard baseline for what factually happened
  ❌ Very dry, provides almost no context, will often just restate official government/authority claims without critical pushback
  No paywall for most content.
- **Reuters**: Similar to AP, with slightly stronger international coverage and the industry gold standard for financial/market news.

---
### 2. For investigative and deep reporting
- **ProPublica**: US non-profit, no partisan affiliation. Publishes rigorously fact-checked, data-driven longform investigations. They release their full raw dataset alongside every major report. It is very rare for their factual claims to be successfully challenged across the political spectrum.
  ❌ Only publishes ~12 major investigations per year, not for daily news.
- **The Guardian**: UK-based global outlet, openly centre-left editorial stance, no billionaire owner. Exceptionally strong on environmental reporting, global human rights and stories ignored by mainstream US outlets. Very transparent about their editorial positions.
  ❌ Framing bias is often present on culture war topics, and opinion writing is frequently mixed into news presentation. No hard paywall.
- **Wall Street Journal**: Right-of-centre editorial board, but their *news desk* (completely separate from opinion) produces extremely high quality business, geopolitical and technology reporting that is trusted even by analysts on the left.
  ❌ Their opinion section is heavily partisan and should be treated as an entirely separate product. Hard paywall.

---
### Critical ground rules for all news:
1.  Avoid any outlet that primarily distributes content through social media algorithm feeds, regardless of their nominal political leaning. All of them will optimize for outrage over accuracy.
2.  Every outlet on this list has gotten major stories wrong before. None should be treated as an unchallenged authority.
3.  To spot bias usefully: Don't ask "is this outlet biased", ask *what does this outlet consistently choose not to report, and who do they always quote as an authoritative source?*

runs.u: Can you recommend a news outlet?
runs.reply:
It's important to first note that no news outlet is entirely free of editorial perspective, potential biases, or contextual limitations. Different outlets operate with varying mandates, ownership backgrounds, and editorial focuses, and it is always advisable to cross-reference information from multiple diverse sources, verify original cited materials, and practice critical media literacy when consuming news.

Here is an overview of different types of outlets with their general characteristics and noted considerations, for you to evaluate based on your needs:
### International wire services (widely used as base sources by many outlets)
1.  **Associated Press (AP)**
    - Profile: A global non-profit wire service, it produces fact-based breaking news and reports on most global events. It is often cited as a primary source by other media.
    - Considerations: It has faced periodic criticism for editorial framing choices in coverage of politically sensitive geopolitical events, and for potential underrepresentation of marginalized community perspectives in some regions.
2.  **Reuters**
    - Profile: An international news agency with broad global coverage, it emphasizes data-backed and factual reporting for both public and industry audiences.
    - Considerations: Critics have noted instances of delayed or cautious framing in coverage of events involving major economic or political stakeholders with which it has commercial ties.

### Regional public service and general news outlets
1.  **BBC News (United Kingdom)**
    - Profile: A publicly funded broadcaster with global news operations, it produces multi-format coverage across most world regions. It operates under a public service mandate for impartial reporting.
    - Considerations: It has faced sustained public and regulatory criticism over alleged bias in domestic political coverage, and over one-sided framing in coverage of select international conflicts.
2.  **Al Jazeera**
    - Profile: Based in Qatar, it provides extensive coverage of events in the Global South that often receive less attention in Western-dominated outlets.
    - Considerations: It has been criticised by some governments and analysts for editorial alignment with Qatari foreign policy positions in Middle East and North African event coverage.

### Important general guidance
- Always review an outlet's public ownership structure, funding sources, and published editorial policies.
- Compare how multiple different outlets report on the same event, paying attention to what facts are emphasized, what sources are cited, and what context is included or omitted.
- No single news outlet should be your exclusive source of information.
